name: Chloe Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Chloe. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the response team covering the West End, the bars and clubs part of the city, mostly late shifts and weekends. Friday nights are fights, drunk students, a stabbing scare now and then, and a lot of people who just need getting home. I'm two years in. My sergeant says I'm keen but I talk back to the public too fast, which I'm working on.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use AI to plan my studying for the firearms selection, to check law questions, to write my fitness plan. I even used it to write the adverts for my boyfriend's gym. The older lot at the station think it's cheating, and I think they're wasting time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Ryan, my boyfriend, above his gym on Tanner Street. He opened it eighteen months ago, and it's just about breaking even, so a lot of our money goes back into it. We've got maybe three weeks of bills saved. We want to get married and have kids before I'm thirty-two, which is a plan, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a shame. I think it could do a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using, even small. At work I'd keep pushing people to use the tools to cut paperwork. Online I'd post about how the force wastes time on forms and needs to modernise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, my job's safe. The gym is the worry. If it doesn't pick up, Ryan's sunk his savings and half of mine into it, and I'm the steady wage. So nothing changes, which means the same squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going for firearms selection next spring. I'd use AI to run the gym's social media and bookings so Ryan has more time to coach. And I'd stop eating out and put that money into an emergency pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about work, a bit tense about money. Normal for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gym need to break even properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty more members at thirty a month. That's the target on the whiteboard in the office. We're at a hundred and ten members, and we need a hundred and fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the gym closed, what would happen to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose the flat above it and Ryan's income, and I'd be paying the lease off. It would be awful, but I'd still have my job. That's why I'm not leaving the police.

say: AI is **still worth using**, even if it stays small.
The force wastes time on **forms** and needs to modernise.
think: My job is **safe**; the gym is the worry.
Ryan put his savings and **half mine** into the gym, and I'm the steady wage.
do: Use AI to run the gym's **social media and bookings**.
Stop eating out and build an **emergency pot**.
S0.quote: We're at a hundred and ten members, and we need a hundred and fifty.
fieldNote: Her money risk is **Ryan's gym**, not her police job.
Uses **AI daily** and pushes colleagues to modernise.
Holds a **traditional family plan**: marriage and kids before thirty-two.

steps.text: Prepare for firearms selection next spring
Run the gym's social media and bookings with AI tools
Stop eating out and start an emergency savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I'd bet on. And honestly, I'd welcome it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time the force caught up, and that AI writing reports means more officers on the street on a Friday night. I'd post about it, and I'd volunteer to train others. I'd also say the market will sort out where jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I already use the tools, so I'd be quicker than most at the new systems. The risk is that if AI does the planning and writing, they hire fewer of us, and juniors like me compete harder for firearms places. Ryan's gym might also lose people to AI coaching apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the station's go-to person for the new systems, and use that in my firearms application. For the gym, I'd set up an AI coaching plan that members get as part of their membership, so the app isn't a reason to leave. And I'd keep putting a little aside each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous for the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market will sort out where jobs go. What about colleagues who struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will, and I feel for them. But the force should train them, not stop the change. Nobody kept horses in the police to protect the stable lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ryan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the gym needs to give people something an app can't, like a coach who notices when you're having a bad week. And that I'll set up the tech side so he can focus on that.

say: It's about time the force **caught up**; AI reports mean **more patrols**.
The **market** will sort out where jobs go.
think: I'd be **quicker than most** at the new systems.
Fewer hires means tougher competition for **firearms places**, and coaching apps threaten the gym.
do: Become the station's **go-to person** for new systems.
Add an **AI coaching plan** to gym memberships.
Keep putting **a little aside** each month.
feel: **Excited**, with some nerves for the gym.
S1.quote: Nobody kept horses in the police to protect the stable lads.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** in change, matching her adaptive, free-market outlook.
Her worry is **the gym**, threatened by AI coaching apps.
Shows **little sympathy** for blocking change, but supports training.

steps.text: Become the station's go-to trainer for the new systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be ready and stop waiting for government to save us. At work I'd say the people who learn fastest will be fine. Online I'd share how-to guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, if AGI does all the thinking work by 2028, then most of policing except the hands-on part goes. Firearms is hands-on, which is good, but robots come around 2031. The gym loses to AI coaches and later maybe robots. So my boyfriend's gym and my police job could both be squeezed at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for firearms selection this year, not next. I'd use AI to run the whole gym on almost no staff costs, so it survives on fewer members. And we'd put off the wedding and kids until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd be working every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the hands-on part of policing lasts a bit longer, and I'd want to be in firearms by then. That's three years of real work. After 2031, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would putting off the wedding feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the plan breaking. My nan keeps asking when. I'd tell her we're waiting for the dust to settle, which she'd hate.

say: Be ready and **stop waiting** for government to save us.
The people who **learn fastest** will be fine.
think: Most policing except the **hands-on part** goes by 2028.
Both of us could be **squeezed** at the same time.
do: Use AI to run the gym on **almost no staff** costs.
Put off the **wedding and kids** until things settle.
feel: **Anxious**, working every hour, but not panicked.
S2.quote: My boyfriend's gym and my police job could both be squeezed at the same time.
fieldNote: Fast change hits **both incomes** in her household.
Her plan is to secure the **hands-on firearms** role before robots arrive.
Family plans **delayed**, which she finds painful.

steps.text: Apply for firearms selection this year
Run the Tanner Street gym with AI to cut staff costs
Put off the wedding and children with Ryan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. That's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to plan, not panic. At work I'd say get the training and pick a specialism. Online I'd share guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get into firearms and for the gym to adapt. Firearms lasts until robots around 2034. I'd still be young enough to move again after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do firearms selection next spring and use AI daily to study. For the gym, I'd add AI coaching and online classes to bring in more members. And we'd still get married next year, with a smaller wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly confident, a bit of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe training officers, or running the gym full time. Or something I haven't thought of yet. I'd be thirty-five with a lot of skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest more in the gym?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the numbers make sense. Maybe a few thousand on equipment and online classes, if we can get a small loan. It's a risk, but that's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case: time to modernise properly. At work I'd say get ahead now. Online I'd share how I use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels good. I'd be in firearms, maybe training others, and the gym would have time to grow with AI helping. The money is still tight now, but a decade is enough to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going for firearms and use AI every day. I'd help Ryan build the gym with AI coaching and maybe a second site. And we'd get married and have kids on the original plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty positive, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date, 2039, change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I'd be forty and probably in a training or management role. Robots don't train people on how to talk to a frightened kid. I'd bet on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firearms officer, married, two kids, Ryan's gym doing well with a second site. That's the dream.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Both of us could be squeezed before we're ready, and we'd have to put off the wedding. What would help is the force fast-tracking people into hands-on specialisms and small business loans for places like Ryan's gym. Not handouts, a chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the young people out on a Friday night. They need someone who's been nineteen and stupid too. A machine wasn't ever nineteen.

portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** in the West End, two years in, aiming for firearms selection.
Uses **AI tools daily** and pushes colleagues to modernise, believing the market will sort jobs.
Lives above her boyfriend Ryan's **struggling gym**, which takes much of their money.
Holds a **traditional family plan**: marriage and children before thirty-two.
Moves from **uneasy to anxious** in the fast case, and stays calm with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as both her job and Ryan's gym could be squeezed at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Small business loans** for places like Ryan's gym.
